triage.rationale: Multiple hosts, 2487 findings spanning high-severity techniques including credential dumping (T1003.*), code execution (T1059.*), process injection (T1134), data destruction (T1490), and lateral movement (T1021.002) form a chained attack pattern unexplained by single rules; IPC$ reconnaissance across multiple source IPs and accounts suggests coordinated reconnaissance or lateral movement within payment infrastructure.

stages.what_happened: A domain-joined workstation's machine account (WE8105DESK$) first touched the IPC$ share on the target server via the 'browser' named pipe, the earliest sign of any client probing this host's shares.

An unauthenticated ANONYMOUS LOGON session from 192.168.2.50 opened the LSA RPC named pipe (lsarpc) on the server, consistent with a null-session probe used to enumerate domain account/policy information before any credentials were presented.
Within two seconds of the anonymous probe, the same source IP re-connected using valid WAYNECORPINC\Administrator credentials, showing the actor had (or obtained) working admin creds for this host.
Using the Administrator session, the actor queried the SAM RPC interface (samr) on the server, a standard step for enumerating local/domain users and groups.

The Administrator session then opened the Service Control Manager named pipe (svcctl), the interface used to remotely create, start, or query Windows services -- typically a precursor to remote command execution.

The same Administrator session subsequently accessed the remote registry named pipe (winreg), which allows reading registry hives over the network and is commonly abused as a precursor to credential-related registry access.

Roughly 20 seconds later, a second wave of ANONYMOUS LOGON connections from 192.168.250.100 repeatedly hit the lsarpc and samr pipes in rapid succession over several seconds, a pattern consistent with an automated account/group enumeration tool rather than manual interactive use.

A final burst of Administrator-authenticated connections from 192.168.2.50 touched additional RPC/service pipes -- srvsvc (share enumeration), winreg, and the previously-unseen DAV RPC SERVICE pipe -- indicating continued host and service discovery using the same compromised admin session.

correlation.summary: Across roughly four minutes, a target server (we9041srv) was probed first by a workstation machine account, then by an unauthenticated null session, then repeatedly by a session authenticated as WAYNECORPINC\Administrator, touching LSA, SAM, Service Control Manager, remote-registry, server-service, and WebClient RPC pipes from two source IPs (192.168.2.50 and 192.168.250.100); the evidence shows a sustained account/service/registry enumeration effort using both anonymous sessions and valid admin credentials, most consistent with an actor mapping accounts, groups, and services on this host in preparation for further action -- the logs do not show evidence of an actual service being created, a payload executed, or data exfiltrated, so any conclusion beyond 'reconnaissance and account/service enumeration' would be speculative.

verdict.headline: Named-pipe telemetry shows a coordinated reconnaissance sweep against we9041srv combining an anonymous null session and WAYNECORPINC\Administrator credentials to enumerate LSA, SAM, service-control, registry, and WebDAV interfaces over about four minutes, with no confirmed evidence in this data of resulting service creation or code execution.

claims.text: The null-session actor at 192.168.250.100 then repeated lsarpc/samr pipe access at least nineteen times within a six-second window (09:33:54-09:33:59), a pattern consistent with automated account/group enumeration tooling rather than manual browsing.

claims.text: Enumeration resumed under WAYNECORPINC\Administrator credentials at 09:34:07, expanding to the server-service (srvsvc) and WebClient/DAV (DAV RPC SERVICE) pipes in addition to further winreg and lsarpc checks, indicating a broadened sweep of remote administrative interfaces on we9041srv.
claims.semantic_support_note: The quoted 'RecordNumber=1084571' is merely a record identifier and carries no semantic content about the claim's specifics, though the surrounding log entry (not the quote itself) does corroborate the srvsvc pipe access at that timestamp under the Administrator account.

claims.text: Every captured event is an EventCode 5145 'access check' audit record whose own message states only that access eligibility was evaluated, not that a resulting RPC call, service installation, or code execution actually occurred, so this evidence set alone does not confirm any follow-on action (e.g., service creation, payload execution) took place.

citations.quoted_span: A network share object was checked to see whether client can be granted desired access.

claims.semantic_support_note: The quoted message text confirms this is indeed a 5145 access-check event stating only that access eligibility was evaluated, with no field indicating an actual RPC call, service installation, or code execution occurred.

verdict.benign_explanation_considered: Routine administrative tooling (RSAT, backup/monitoring agents, vulnerability scanners) can legitimately touch lsarpc/samr/svcctl/winreg pipes on a Windows host, and the initial WE8105DESK$ browser-pipe check could be ordinary NetBIOS browsing traffic. This does not explain the anonymous NT AUTHORITY\ANONYMOUS LOGON null session querying LSA/SAM, which normal domain-joined management tools do not use, nor the sub-six-second repetition rate of that burst, which is more consistent with scripted enumeration than human or standard-agent activity; the benign explanation therefore survives only for the earliest machine-account event, not for the null-session and admin-credential enumeration that follows.

proposals.justification: Confirm or rule out downstream service creation or process execution following the LSA/SAM/svcctl/winreg pipe enumeration before escalating to disruptive containment.

Check threat intel on the source IP that carried both anonymous LSA/SAM probing and Administrator-credentialed svcctl/winreg access to establish whether it is a known internal admin host or an attacker pivot point.
Escalate the coordinated null-session plus Administrator-credential reconnaissance sweep against we9041srv for human review given moderate confidence and recorded counter-evidence.

The Administrator account was used within the same four-minute window as an anonymous null session to enumerate LSA, SAM, service-control, and registry pipes on we9041srv, warranting revocation of its active sessions across the observed hosts pending investigation, without isolating either host outright given no confirmed execution.

banner: This incident had 2487 findings; the investigation examined the first 40. The verdict above, if any, is scoped to what was examined.

lyzr_triage.rationale: The multi-host, high-volume detections combine credential theft, remote execution, injection, and recovery inhibition, indicating a coordinated compromise requiring investigation.
